quote: Expressive content contributes a dimension of meaning that is separate from the regular descriptive content.
note: Members the paper names: damn, bastard (p. 165); fucking (pp. 166, 187); nigger (p. 181); honky (p. 173); Köter (p. 170); Japanese chimau- (p. 168); Japanese honorifics; German formal/familiar pronoun features (§4); swear words; racial epithets; curses. Borderline: German ja, evidentials.

quote: The facts suggest that expressive content is not propositional, that it is distinct from the meanings we typically assign to sentences.
So expressives do not change the descriptive content at all.
Expressives cannot (outside of direct quotation) be used to report on past events, attitudes, or emotions, nor can they express mere possibilities, conjectures, or suppositions.
As we have seen, essen- tially no kind of syntactic embedding delivers the possibility of a semanti- cally embedded interpretation.
note: The only negation tests are (8a) *isn't* and (8b) *It's just false that*. Both use the integrated epithet *that bastard Kresge*, which is not among the 46. Host relation: integrated.

quote: In general, the perspective is the speaker’s, but there can be deviations if conditions are right.

note: The text goes on: angry or elated, frustrated or at ease, powerful or subordinated. The last pair is social (honorification) rather than affective.

quote: Speakers are never fully satisﬁed when they paraphrase expressive content using descriptive, i.e., nonexpressive, terms.
